text:
In the spring of 1546, the French ambassador was meeting secretly with Ottoman envoys in Venice. The negotiations were conducted by Gabriel de Luetz, who was known for his discretion. There were several reasons for this caution. Francis was not willing to admit the alliance publicly, since it was considered scandalous by most of Christendom.

Historians have long argued that the alliance was purely pragmatic. Braudel argues that the Mediterranean was a single economic space, his argument has been widely accepted. This is important because it reframes the question. Having read the dispatches, the alliance appears more ideological than previously thought. The decision was made by the king to send a second embassy, of course.

The transformation of the court became visible in the 1540s. It was a period in which patronage was being redistributed. Montmorency's fall was the result of a long rivalry. The study of the correspondence of the secretaries of the king reveals a different picture. The king did not remember the promise he had made to the Venetians.
